title: OPTEVFOR Tests New Landing System on USS Abraham Lincoln
description: The F-35C Lightning II aircraft are the next step in the Navy’s plan for air dominance and are still undergoing various tests. Petty Officer Brian M. Brooks says the latest test for the fifth-generation aircraft uses technology that hits pretty close to home.
keywords: F-35, USS Abraham Lincoln, CVN 72, Strike Fighter Squadron 125, (VFA 125), F35-C, Raytheon, F-35C Lightning II, PO2 Brian M. Brooks, COMOPTEVFOR, OT1, JPALS, Petty Officer 1st Class Brian M. Brooks, MC1 Brian M. Brooks, Operational Test and Evaluation Force, OPTEVFOR, Commander Operational Test and Evaluation Force, Joint Precision Approach and Landing System, carrier qualifications. CQ, Operational Test 1

transcript.text: - [Brian] The Navy is testing this next generation aircraft,
the F-35C Lighting II aboard USS Abraham Lincoln.
One of the very fundamental tests for these pilots
is simply landing and stopping on the deck
of this floating city, and as research has shown,
it's not always an easy thing to do.
- I'd heard stories that during Vietnam they hooked
a bunch of stress sensors up to aviators,
and sent them out into combat and they were checking
respiration, pulse rate, blood pressure,
sweating, things of that nature.
And they found out that, yes,
being shot at in combat was pretty stressful,
but the most stressful thing these aviators did
was land on the carrier at nighttime.
That would peg all the readings.
And you may not always drop bombs,
you may not always be in combat, but you always
have to land on a ship at night.
- [Brian] So to help the pilots, the Navy implemented
various electronic signal systems, such as radar,
to assist them in landing.
Commander Operational Test and Evaluation Force,
or COMOPTEVFOR, the Navy's sole operational test agency,
sent out one of it's contractors,
along with a technician from Ratheon,
to collect data on the newest system being tested,
called Joint Precision Approach and Landing Systems,
or JPALS, which uses technology
we're all familiar with, GPS.
- There's five sensors spread throughout the ship
that collect GPS data, our algorithms process it
and tries to find the best solution, user position solution
or ship position solution and it sends
that data out to the air crafts,
and it's a one way data link with the F35.
- [Brian] The theory behind JPALS,
is through the use of GPS, the plane will receive
a more accurate position of the ship upon approach.
But that's not the only improvement JPALS can offer.
- One thing that's significant about JPALS,
is JPALS is not yet a complete replacement,
but very well-integrated into existing systems
so it allows us to use capabilities
and strengths of the old system with the capability
and new strengths of JPALS now.
- [Brian] USS Abraham Lincoln is currently
the only aircraft carrier with JPALS installed
into their landing system, and is currently underway
conducting carrier qualifications with not only
the F35s, but with FA18 Super Hornets as well.
- What works out nicely is that F35 was also
out here doing their own testing, and the results
from both the JPALS test and the F35 test
goes through COMOPTEVFOR, then from
our Admiral at COMOPTEVFOR on up to
the Chief of Naval Operations to go make the decision
based on the test results as to whether or not
they want to continue purchasing and using the systems.
- [Brian] These types of first hand
operational tests performed by COMOPTEVFOR
provide real data from the war fighters
to help shape future systems.
- It means a lot being able to have people
directly on board that can, that you can interface with
in real time, instead of having to reach out,
make phone calls after the fact.
But having them actually on board to give us feedback
and or corrections for later on is a tremendous help
to make the JPALS implementation progress smooth.
- [Brian] Petty Officer Brian M. Brooks,
USS Abraham Lincoln.
